say: Welcome, Factor Hunters! Every number hides its factors inside it, and today we hunt them all down, without missing a single one.
We will also find out when two buses meet again, and why some numbers have an odd number of factors. Notice it. Test it. Explain why.
We count round the group, one number each. If your number is in the 3 times table, say "Fizz". In the 4 times table, say "Buzz". In both, say "Fizz-Buzz"!
If you slip, no problem: say "My go again" and pick someone to start the next round.
Before we start: which will be the first Fizz-Buzz number? Write your guess on your whiteboard.
You have 24 square tiles. You must use all of them to make one rectangle. How many different rectangles do you think you can make? Write your guess.
stuck: Stuck: start with one long row. How many tiles in the row? Now try 2 rows.
Not sure if 4 by 6 and 6 by 4 are different: turn your rectangle round. Is it the same shape?
Finished early: do it again with 36 tiles. Something special happens. What is it?

say: “Factor pairs of 36. I try 1, 2, 3 in order. 1 × 36. 2 × 18. 3 × 12. 4 × 9. Does 5 work? No, 36 is not in the 5 times table. 6 × 6. The next number, 9, is already in a pair, so the pairs have met. I stop. 36 has 9 factors.”

“12 apples and 18 oranges in identical bags, nothing left over. The number of bags must be a factor of 12 AND a factor of 18. The common factors are 1, 2, 3, 6. The most bags is 6, with 2 apples and 3 oranges in each.”
“Buses every 6 minutes and every 8 minutes. I list the multiples: 6, 12, 18, 24 … and 8, 16, 24. The first number in both lists is 24, so they meet again after 24 minutes, not 48.”

do: Ask: “How do you know you have found every factor pair? Where did you stop?”
Ask: “Is that a factor or a multiple? Which is bigger?”
Ask: “Which list did you write: the factors, or the multiples? Which do you need for this question?”
stuck: Hint 1: “Try 1, 2, 3, 4 … in order. Does it go in exactly?”
Hint 2: “Draw the rectangles, or make them with tiles.”
Hint 3: “Write the first few multiples of each number in two rows. Circle the numbers in both rows.”

say: “Ali says: bigger numbers always have more factors. Who agrees? Can you find an example that proves him wrong?”
ask: “Ali says: bigger numbers always have more factors. Who agrees? Can you find an example that proves him wrong?”
Ali is wrong. 24 has 8 factors but 29, which is bigger, has only 2 (1 and 29).

say: “Today you hunted factors in order, so none could hide. You found common factors for sharing and common multiples for timetables.”
“Hand me your exit ticket and I will stamp your inquiry journal.”

p4l1-title.note: Objective: Find all the factor pairs of a number by working in order, find common factors (sharing into identical packs) and common multiples (when do buses meet again), discover which numbers have an odd number of factors, and solve multiple-based logic riddles. Thinking strategies taught today: MAKE A LIST IN ORDER, LOOK FOR A PATTERN and USE THE CLUES ONE AT A TIME. Materials: 36 square tiles or squared paper per pair, mini whiteboards, coloured pencils, a 1 to 50 number strip. Online: children cut 24 paper squares (or use squared paper) before the lesson and build rectangles on camera; the tutor marks the bus time line and the factor rainbow on the slides. Time plan (90 minutes in all; every part has a budget and there is a 3-minute standing buffer inside the page-2 block). Opening 0 to 1.5. Sneak-peek puzzles 1.5 to 7 (puzzle 1 about 60 seconds, puzzle 2 about 90 seconds, then ONE check moment for both puzzles; answers ticked or said together on three; nothing held up to the camera, nobody marked). Warm-up game 7 to 9 (one short round, about 90 seconds), quick questions 9 to 12.5 (three questions). Explore 12.5 to 24.5 (the only breakout of the first half: about 60 seconds each way, closed by a 60-second timer; a Go further what-if is on the slide from the start; two debrief questions). Teaching 24.5 to 32.5 (click to reveal each step and answer; the one "your turn" slide is optional: skip it if you are behind). Brain break 32.5 to 36 (water and toilet first, then the game; clock check at the end of the break: if you are more than 1.5 minutes behind, skip the next optional item, never a check, the exit ticket or Looking back). Worksheet 36 to 79.5: page 1 (Start here, in pairs) 36 to 54, check together 54 to 56.5, short teaching before page 2 56.5 to 60, page 2 on your own 60 to 77 (the last 3 minutes are the standing buffer: if earlier parts ran long, spend the buffer first, then the choice questions, and never the checks, the exit ticket or Looking back), check together 77 to 79.5. Talk time 79.5 to 83 (one minute of pair talk, no breakout). Exit ticket 83 to 86.5. Looking back 86.5 to 90 (2 minutes of writing). After question 3 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder. Think harder, Go further and the Investigation have no fixed time slot: any child may choose them at any time, or take them home. The tutor never announces who is on which page, and pairs are not split unless both children agree. Online: page 1 is pair work, so allow about 2 minutes to move into and out of breakout rooms (or run page 1 as a whole-group screen-share if there are only 8 children).

p4l1-check.note: Minutes 1.5 to 7 (5.5 minutes). SNEAK-PEEK PUZZLES. Say: "These are ideas we have not learnt yet. Guessing is welcome, drawing is welcome and so is saying I do not know. Nobody is marked, and nobody's answer is shown to the group." Puzzle 1 is a TRY IT puzzle: any child can start it with objects, a drawing or counting, so everyone has a first win. Puzzle 2 needs a little thinking. Give about 60 seconds for puzzle 1 and about 90 seconds for puzzle 2. Children show their answers PRIVATELY: written on their own paper and said together on three (nothing is held up to the camera). Make ONE check for both puzzles, after puzzle 2: children say the answers together on three. Never use private chat or DMs. Never ask for boards or paper held up in front of the group or to the camera, never read out whose answer is whose, and never say who got it right. Then click to show each answer and talk it through for everyone ("some of you tried ..."), naming no child. Nobody is called on by name, and passing is always fine. ANSWERS: 1) Any one of these is right: 1 bag of 12, 2 bags of 6, 3 bags of 4, 4 bags of 3, 6 bags of 2 or 12 bags of 1. The numbers of sweets in a bag (1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12) are the factors of 12. A child with one way has had a win. 2) Floors 15 and 30. They are in both lists: they are the multiples of 15. A GOOD REASON: A factor goes INTO a number (the sweets in each bag). A multiple is in a times table (the lift floors). Write both lists and look for what they share. Use what you see only to plan your help. It does not decide who is on which page and it is not recorded as a mark. ON PAGE 1 (printed): "After question 3 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder." Make the invitation to the WHOLE group ("when you have finished Start here you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation"), so nobody is singled out. Never message a child privately, never name a child, and never announce who is on which page. Everyone stays in the same room and every child turns to the page they choose. If a pair would be split, ask both children first; never leave a child alone on page 1 (join them to another pair or to yourself).

p4l1-warm1.note: Minutes 7 to 9 (one short round, about 90 seconds: the Sneak-peek puzzles came first). Fizz-Buzz. Count round the group (online: in the order of the video tiles), one number each. A multiple of 3 is "Fizz", a multiple of 4 is "Buzz", a multiple of both is "Fizz-Buzz". A child who slips just says "my go again" and carries on: no one is out and nobody is counted. Stop at about 90 seconds, even if it is going well. The guess is in the SAY line. Then click: the teal boxes are the multiples of 3, the red lines the multiples of 4, and yellow shows the numbers in both: 12 and 24. The next Fizz-Buzz is 36: they go up in 12s. Introduce the words: 12 is a MULTIPLE of 3 and of 4, so it is a COMMON MULTIPLE. That idea comes back with the buses later.

p4l1-warm2.note: Minutes 9 to 12.5. Three questions, about 30 seconds each: read each aloud, write it, say the answer together on three, then click to show. No follow-up questions: if a child raises it, a factor goes INTO a number (56 is a multiple of 7), and 12 is the smallest common multiple of 4 and 6. Answers: yes, 6 12 18 24 30, 12 (or 24, 36). The other two warm-up questions (Is 45 a multiple of 4? Write 18 as a product, 3 ways) are in the Weekly Dose of Thinking Math.

p4l1-explore1.note: Minutes 12.5 to 21.5. Pairs build rectangles with 24 tiles (online: paper squares or squared paper on camera). Ask for a prediction first: how many rectangles? Most guess too many or too few. Let them build in any order at first; the teaching part shows how to work in order. Go further (on the slide), for any child who wants it: do it again with 36 tiles. Something special happens (a 6 by 6 square). What is it? GO FURTHER (on the slide from the start of the explore, so nobody waits): What if we use 36 tiles? What is special about one of the rectangles? Answer: 5 rectangles: 1 × 36, 2 × 18, 3 × 12, 4 × 9 and 6 × 6. The 6 × 6 is a square: 6 is its own partner, so 36 has an odd number (9) of factors.

p4l1-explore2.note: Minutes 21.5 to 24.5. Pencils down (or when the 60-second timer closes the rooms), then gather. Two debrief questions only. Collect the rectangles in the order children say them, then ask: "Is anything missing? Is anything there twice?" Answers: 1) 4 rectangles: 1 × 24, 2 × 12, 3 × 8, 4 × 6. 2) Try 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 rows in order. 5 rows does not work (24 is not in the 5 times table). 6 rows is the 4 × 6 turned round, so we can stop. The third question (what do the side lengths tell us about 24?) is answered by the first teaching slide: they are the factors of 24. With 36 tiles there are 5 rectangles, and one is a square (6 × 6). Do NOT teach the rainbow yet: the next slides do.

p4l1-teach1.note: Teach. This slide answers the third explore question: the side lengths of the rectangles are the factors of 24. Point at the array: "3 rows of 8 make 24." Click through. Think-aloud: "A factor goes INTO a number with nothing left over. A multiple is what you get when you multiply, so it is in the times table." Ask before step 3: "Is 5 a factor of 24? How could you check?" (divide, or look at the 5 times table: 20, 25; 24 is not there). Last line: a quick way to catch a mix-up. 24 has factors up to 24, and multiples from 24 upwards.

p4l1-we1.note: Make a list in order: today's main strategy. Click to add each row while children say it first on whiteboards. Think-aloud: "1 × 36. 2 goes into 36: 2 × 18. 3 × 12. 4 × 9. Does 5 go into 36? No, 36 is not in the 5 times table, so I skip it. 6 × 6. The next number to try is 7, then 8, then 9, but 9 is already in my list (4 × 9). The pairs have met, so I stop." Then click for the factor rainbow: each arch joins a factor pair. 6 has no partner because 6 × 6 uses it twice, so 36 has an odd number of factors (9). We come back to that before page 2.

p4l1-we2.note: Teach before worksheet page 1 (Q3 is the same kind of puzzle). Ask first: "Could we use 4 bags?" (4 goes into 12 but not into 18: 2 oranges would be left over). Click through. Think-aloud: "Every bag is the same, and nothing is left over, so the number of bags must go into 12 exactly AND into 18 exactly. That is a common factor." Click the bags to check: 6 × 2 = 12 apples, 6 × 3 = 18 oranges.

p4l1-we3.note: Click to draw the jumps of 6 (teal, above), then the jumps of 8 (red, below), then circle where both land. Think-aloud: "Bus A leaves at 6, 12, 18, 24 minutes past 7. Bus B at 8, 16, 24. The first number in both lists is 24, the smallest common multiple of 6 and 8." Ask: "Ravi says 6 × 8 = 48, so they meet at 7:48. Is he right?" (They DO meet at 48, but they meet first at 24. Multiplying gives a common multiple, not always the first one.)

p4l1-try2.note: Whiteboards. a) 4, 8, 12 and 6, 12: 12 seconds (not 24). b) 4, 8, 12, 16, 20 and 10, 20: 20 days (not 40). c) 3, 6, 9, 12, 15 and 5, 10, 15: 15. Ask a child to explain why b is not 40.

p4l1-key.note: Say the key idea together. Common mistakes to watch for during the worksheet: (1) Listing factors at random and missing one, or stopping too early (for 48, forgetting 6 × 8), instead of trying 1, 2, 3 … in order until the pairs meet. (2) Mixing up factors and multiples: saying 12 is a factor of 4. (3) For common multiples, multiplying the two numbers every time (10 × 15 = 150 minutes) instead of listing the multiples to find the first one they share (30).

p4l1-break.note: 3.5 minutes: water and toilet FIRST (about one minute), then the game (about two minutes), then back in your seats. CLOCK CHECK at the end of the break (minute 36): if you are more than 1.5 minutes behind, skip the next optional item (the "your turn" slide, a second speaker-note question), never a check, the exit ticket or Looking back. Call numbers such as 30, 45, 60, 100, 72, 15. Online: hands up for stand, hands down for sit. Ask: "Which numbers made everyone stand for 3, 4 AND 5?" (60: a common multiple of 3, 4 and 5).

p4l1-ws1.note: Minutes 36 to 54. Walk around. Ask "How do you know you have them all?" before giving any help. Q2 is the rectangles idea again, but the stem now says 2 rows of 20 and 20 rows of 2 are different ways to plant (unlike the explore, where a turned rectangle did not count), so both count. Point children to that sentence. Q3c: check that each pack has the same number of each colour. CHOOSING (printed on page 1: "After question 3 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder."): invite the WHOLE group ("when you have finished Start here you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation"); never message a child privately, never name a child, never announce who is on which page. If one child of a pair wants to move on, do not split the pair unless both agree; if a pair does lose a member, join the other child to another pair or to yourself straight away. Children on Think harder keep working through the page check; reading along is optional.

p4l1-ws1ans.note: Click each answer after a pair explains theirs. Q1c: 7 does not go into 48 and the next factor, 8, is already in the pair 6 × 8. Q2: the rows can be 2, 4, 5, 8, 10 or 20 (factors of 40 apart from 1 and 40). Q3: 18 ÷ 6 = 3 red and 24 ÷ 6 = 4 blue in each pack.

p4l1-teachodd.note: Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q5 counts factors). Click to list the pairs of 100 and of 18. Point out that 100 has an odd number of factors (9) because 10 is its own partner. Numbers like 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 100 are a number times itself, called square numbers: they make square arrays, like the 6 by 6 square from the explore. 81 = 9 × 9: pairs 1 × 81, 3 × 27, 9 × 9, so 5 factors. Do not list the numbers with exactly 3 factors: that is Q5c.

p4l1-teachriddle.note: Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q6a). Use the clues one at a time and make a list. Ask before step 1: "Which numbers are multiples of both 3 and 5?" Some children will list the 3s and the 5s and circle the numbers in both; that works too. Think-aloud: "After each clue my list gets shorter. When only one number is left, I check it against EVERY clue."

p4l1-teachtest.note: Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q6b asks who is right). Ask the group to vote before clicking. Think-aloud: "To show something is ALWAYS true I need a reason, like 4 = 2 × 2. To show it is NOT always true I only need one example that breaks it." For children who are quick: every multiple of 10 is a multiple of 5, but not the other way round (15).

p4l1-ws2.note: Children work alone. Note who needs a short catch-up next lesson, especially children who still mix up factors and multiples. SOLO PAGE CAP: Page 2 is on your own. Aim for Q4 and Q5 first. Q6 is a choice for the last few minutes. Children who finish choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation; nobody is told which. BUFFER: the last 3 minutes of this block (minute 74 to 77) are the standing buffer. If earlier parts ran long, page 2 starts late and the buffer is spent first, then the choice questions at the end of the page. Never shorten the checks, the exit ticket or Looking back. Say nothing about the buffer to the children.

p4l1-ws2ans.note: Click after a child explains. Q4: Bus 33 at :00, :10, :20, :30; Bus 51 at :00, :15, :30. They meet every 30 minutes. Q5c: 49 = 7 × 7, so its factors are 1, 7 and 49: exactly 3. A number with exactly 3 factors is a number times itself where that number has only 2 factors: 2 × 2, 3 × 3, 5 × 5, 7 × 7. 16 = 4 × 4 has 5 factors, and 36 has 9. Finding ALL such numbers from 1 to 60 (4, 9, 25, 49) is Think harder Q4. Q6a: multiples of 12 between 30 and 70 are 36, 48, 60; 48 is a multiple of 8; in 60 the ones digit is smaller than the tens digit.

p4l1-stretch.note: Answers (same four questions as the printed Think harder page): 1) 12 factors: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 12, 18, 24, 36, 72. 2) 18 seconds (6, 12, 18 and 9, 18). 3) 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12 4) 4, 9, 25 and 49. Each is a number times itself (2 × 2, 3 × 3, 5 × 5, 7 × 7), where that number has only 2 factors. 16 = 4 × 4 has 5 factors and 36 has 9.

p4l1-challenge.note: Pairs try first, then use the "see it" slide if stuck, then the walk-through. These are Go further Q7 and Q6. Answers: 1) Lockers 1, 4, 9 and 16: each locker is changed once for every factor of its number, and only numbers with an odd number of factors end up open. 2) 61: one less than the number is a common multiple of 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6, which is 60.

p4l1-chdiag.note: Show after pairs have tried Go further, or if they are stuck. The pictures show the problem, not the answer. Ask: For Q1, which children touch locker 6? Locker 9? What do those numbers have to do with factors? For Q2, if you take away the 1 that is left over, what kind of number is left? Answers are in the Go further slide notes.

p4l1-chwalk.note: Use after pairs have tried. Q1: act out locker 6 and locker 9 with a door (a book cover) opening and closing. Every factor pair gives two changes, so a locker ends up closed, unless its number is something times itself: 1, 4, 9, 16. Q2: check 61: 61 = 2 × 30 + 1 = 3 × 20 + 1 = 4 × 15 + 1 = 5 × 12 + 1 = 6 × 10 + 1.

p4l1-talk.note: Minutes 79.5 to 83. Pair talk is 1 minute (no breakout rooms: children tell the grown-up beside them, or write one sentence), then share. Answer: Ali is wrong. 24 has 8 factors, but 29, which is bigger, has only 2 (1 and 29). One example is enough to show he is wrong (like Siti's claim earlier). Not asked in class (moved to the Weekly Dose of Thinking Math): "Why did the 36-tile rectangles give an odd number of factors?" (6 × 6: 6 is its own partner). Praise the reasons, not only the answers. TALK TIME RULES: ask for volunteers first; a child may always pass; never call on a child by name to answer; no public tallies, scores or rankings; praise the reason, not the child. If a question uses a mistaken idea (a character who gets it wrong), present it as the character's idea and ask "What would you say to them?" so no child owns the mistake.

p4l1-exit.note: Minutes 83 to 86.5. Answer: 1, 2, 4, 7, 14, 28. The smallest common multiple of 6 and 9 is 18 (6, 12, 18 and 9, 18). Extension: which numbers from 1 to 50 have exactly 4 factors? (15 numbers: 6, 8, 10, 14, 15, 21, 22, 26, 27, 33, 34, 35, 38, 39, 46.)

p4l1-reflect.note: Minutes 86.5 to 90 (2 minutes of writing, 3.5 minutes with the routine). LOOKING BACK. Children fill in the box on the Investigation page, the page every child has (something I did well; the hardest part was; what helped me; one thing I could try next). Say one sentence: "Turn to page 3, the Looking back box. Write, tick or pass. Two minutes, no talking." The printed box says the rest. Model one yourself first: "Something I did well: I wrote the factor pairs in order. The hardest part was knowing when to stop listing factors. What helped me: writing the pairs in order and asking my partner. One thing I could try next: making a table of the factor pairs." Say: "Ticking I am still stuck is a good thing to do: it tells me where to help." Do not ask anyone to read theirs out. If a child wants to share, take one volunteer and thank them for the strategy. Never grade it, never correct it, never collect it for marks and never show it to the group. Never ask a child to hold a page to the camera. Never ask for photos or private messages. If I am still stuck is ticked, check in during the open session: a quick visit to the shared breakout room or a hand signal, with a parent nearby. Never send a DM. Praise strategies ("you drew it", "you asked for help"), not speed or scores.
